one_liner: Rust-core Python quadtree for points and boxes; NumPy-return path about 35x faster than Rtree, 4.5x than Shapely STRtree.
what_it_does: fastquadtree is a pip-installable Python package (PyO3/maturin wheels, no runtime dependencies) that exposes a Rust region quadtree over fixed root bounds. QuadTree stores points with integer IDs, RectQuadTree stores bounding boxes, and the *Objects variants attach Python objects. Each supports insert/insert_many/insert_many_np, delete, rectangle range query (query returns Python lists, query_np returns NumPy arrays), nearest_neighbor(s), and to_bytes/from_bytes serialization. Coordinates can be f32 (default), f64, i32 or i64. It is not API-compatible with Rtree or Shapely STRtree, but it ships a drop-in fastquadtree.pyqtree.Index shim and a mostly drop-in pygame sprite Group.
how_it_is_fast: The tree is a plain pointer-based region quadtree in Rust: leaves hold up to capacity items in a Vec, then split into four children (Box<[QuadTree; 4]>) down to a dtype-dependent max depth, and deletes merge underfull nodes locally. Range queries walk the tree iteratively with a SmallVec stack and switch to report-all mode for nodes fully inside the window, which skips per-item tests. Queries release the GIL and collect results into flat Rust vectors, and query_np hands them back as NumPy arrays instead of building per-hit Python tuples; most of the speedup over pure-Python quadtrees and over the list path comes from avoiding Python object creation. The release build uses opt-level 3, thin LTO, codegen-units=1 and panic=abort.
when_to_use: Python programs that index many 2D points or boxes and run many window queries, especially with NumPy arrays on both sides (insert_many_np in, query_np out)
Replacing pyqtree without code changes: the shim measured 1.127 s versus 11.647 s for the original on 500,000 items and 500 queries
Games and simulations (pygame broadphase culling, moving-object collision) with frequent inserts and deletes inside known fixed bounds
Caching or sharing a prebuilt index across processes: rebuilding 1M points from bytes took 7.1 ms versus 88.8 ms to reinsert them
Pyodide/WebAssembly or ARM targets: wheels exist for manylinux x86_64/aarch64/armv7l, macOS universal2, Windows amd64 and Pyodide wasm32
when_not_to_use: C++ or Rust consumers: it is a Python extension with no documented C/C++ or Rust API (a Rust API request, issue #11, was closed without a visible answer)
When results must come back as Python lists: the list path's query time (0.231 s) loses to Shapely STRtree (0.110 s) and total time is only about 1.08x better (derived from page data)
Data that can fall outside the initial root bounds: bounds are fixed, out-of-bounds inserts are rejected, and dynamic root bounds (issue #17) were closed as not planned
Large-k nearest-neighbour queries: nearest_neighbors(k) reruns a full single-nearest search k times while excluding already-picked IDs, so cost grows with k
Polygons or exact geometry predicates: only points and axis-aligned boxes are indexed; use Shapely STRtree or GEOS for geometry-level tests

integration.dependencies: none at runtime (NumPy optional, for the *_np methods); Rust build dependencies: pyo3 0.28 (abi3-py39), numpy 0.28, smallvec, wincode, num-traits
integration.min_toolchain: Python 3.9+ (CPython, abi3 wheels); building from source needs Rust 1.89+ and maturin
integration.platforms: Prebuilt wheels for Linux x86_64/aarch64/armv7l (manylinux_2_28), macOS x86_64/arm64, Windows amd64, Pyodide wasm32; no SIMD-specific code
integration.thread_safety: not documented; queries release the GIL, and PyO3's per-call borrow checking means a mutation from another thread during a query should raise an error rather than corrupt the tree (inferred from the bindings, not stated)
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — fastquadtree.pyqtree.Index is a drop-in for PyQtree, but the API differs from Rtree (libspatialindex) and Shapely STRtree

gotchas: The default dtype is f32, so large projected or geographic coordinates lose precision; pass dtype='f64' when you need it

With dtype i32 or i64, squared distances in nearest-neighbour search are computed in the coordinate type itself. The release profile does not enable overflow checks, so i32 trees should return wrong neighbours once distances exceed about 46,340 units (from reading geom.rs and Cargo.toml, not tested)

insert_many raises TypeError on NumPy input, so you must call insert_many_np explicitly. Containment is half-open (min inclusive, max exclusive), so points exactly on the max edge of the root bounds are rejected

Serialized blobs are version-sensitive: data written by bincode-based releases (v2.2 and earlier) cannot be loaded by current wincode-based ones, and from_bytes enforces a 64 MiB preallocation limit unless you raise it
pick_this_over_siblings_when: The catalogued siblings are C++/Rust/JS libraries (nanoflann, PH-tree, KDBush, RBush, geo-index), none callable from Python as a drop-in; pick fastquadtree when you are in Python and need a mutable point/box index with NumPy I/O. Pick geo-index or a C++ kd-tree such as nanoflann for static data in compiled code.
verified_claims_summary: The first-party cross-library benchmark (CPython 3.14.5, AMD Ryzen 7 3700X, CachyOS; rustc version not stated) builds 500,000 random integer points in a 1000x1000 box (so many duplicates) and runs 500 random windows, many of them large, taking the median of 3 repeats. Totals: fastquadtree query_np 0.068 s, list path 0.285 s, Shapely STRtree 0.309 s, Rtree 2.351 s and PyQtree 2.909 s, so about 34.6x over Rtree and 4.5x over STRtree with NumPy returns (derived from page data). Rtree was built by stream bulk-loading 1x1 boxes from a Python generator, STRtree's build time includes converting the Python list to NumPy and Shapely points, and query cost is dominated by materializing results.
status_note: Active single-maintainer project (v2.4.2 on PyPI 2026-06-22, 303 commits, 33 stars, 7 issues all closed), MIT-licensed, with 100% test coverage claimed; usable from Python only.
